cells.tense: What you have tended is bearing fruit right now, and you are still standing in the garden.
cells.act: let the friction test what you are committed to
cells.ask: Take the part of what you tend that would hurt most to lose, and give it your attention this week even on the day it goes dull. Keep going past the tedious stretch.
cells.core:
You tend things and they come up. That isn't luck; it's that you stay after the interesting part is over, and what you stay with gets large enough for other people to see. Around you, small things are allowed to be small, and you don't need them to be more yet. That patience is the whole mechanism.

Somewhere in what you feed there's a part that would hurt more than the others to lose. Feed that part first this week, before the rest, even when it asks for something boring. What needs care doesn't announce itself, and the others can wait seven days. What you chose will show you what your attention has been doing.
cells.sheetLine: What you stay with grows where people can see it.
cells.verb: Tending what is growing, past the point where it still needs you
cells.place: Where everything is still possible and nothing has been decided

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead of you the things you tend will have to prove they were worth it, and you are already out there waiting.
cells.act: join someone in the work so the two streams run as one
cells.ask: Bring another person into something you're growing and do a single piece of the work alongside them this week — no plan, no report, just the shared task.
cells.core:
You keep something open on purpose, and there's real care in that. But staying open has started to run past the thing itself: each season you leave it undecided a little longer, so nothing has to become what it is and be tended as that. From your side it reads as patience.

Let another person in on it. Not to hand it over — to work beside you on a single piece this week, and let what they do stand as it is. You'll find out what the thing actually needs, which is different from what you imagine it will need. Two hands on it also means the ground you've kept bare can finally be planted.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it open a little longer than it needs.

cells.tense: After everything you tended, you have been standing past the harvest and looking back at it.
cells.act: choose which star to steer by and steer
cells.ask: Settle on a direction for what you tend and hold it for three days — same heading each morning, nothing surveyed, nothing re-decided after the first call.
cells.core:
Somewhere in your life you still care for things, but you've come loose from the front of it. What you tended already did what it was going to do, and you're on the far side of that, answering each day as it arrives rather than steering anything. There's no new thing in your hands, and part of you is waiting for one.

You don't need the whole garden back. You need a direction. Take what you tend, settle where it should go, and hold that heading for three days without re-arguing it every morning. Wanting is allowed to be the reason; it doesn't have to survive a debate. A heading is not a promise about how the days will go.

cells.tense: Things around you are growing because you keep showing up, and you'd describe almost none of it as yours.
cells.act: release the method, not the purpose
cells.ask: Next time something you tend stops answering your usual approach, name what you're actually trying to give it — hold that, and drop the method you've been using.
cells.core:
You are the one who waters and waits, and you have been filing it under circumstances: a good season, a lucky run, someone else's timing. Meanwhile the people and things that grew did so where you stood, and they know whose tending it was. The hand is doing the work and the name on it is missing.

Next time what you tend stops answering the method, don't conclude you've lost your touch. Say what you're trying to give it, and keep that, dropping only the approach. What you release was not the point; the care is. Naming what you meant to give is how you find that you knew it.

attempts.check: The draft risks claiming the person has actually harvested something abundant — the record only says the capacity for letting things grow unattended is what's operating, and a reader could fairly say 'nothing of mine has flourished.' The asks survive that: watering what you'd be sorriest to lose, doing something whole with one other person, picking a heading, and letting friction test a commitment all teach something about tending even if the reading is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about abundance arriving, so I've kept the fruit out of every cell and left only the tending.
